Abstract Fulgurites are natural glasses formed when cloud-to-ground lightning fuses sand, soil, rock, or related substrates. Pasek, Block, and Pasek describe fulgurites as natural glasses produced by lightning and classify their morphologies across sand, clay, caliche, rock, and related forms. This write-up argues that structural nitrogen, meaning nitrogen bonded directly into the silica network as Si–N or Si–O–N, should not be expected in ordinary terrestrial fulgurite glass. The reason is mechanistic: ordinary fulgurites form in air, in oxidizing conditions, and quench rapidly. Experimental work on nitrogen in silicate melts shows that nitrogen behavior is strongly controlled by oxygen fugacity; over broad conditions N₂ is the dominant dissolved species, while N³⁻-type structural species become significant only under reducing conditions. The useful chemistry contribution is therefore not “we found structural nitrogen.” The stronger contribution is a provenance protocol: separate nitrogen into lattice, gas, surface, and organic reservoirs; test each with the right instrument; state an upper bound when the bonding test is mute; and avoid false positives from surface contamination, organic matter, SIMS recombination, or modern air infiltration. The two most promising positive archive lanes are: first, sealed-vesicle gas, because Navarro-González and colleagues reported CO₂, CO, and NO in glassy bubbles from a Late Pleistocene Libyan Desert fulgurite; and second, carbon-correlated reduced phases, because lightning has been shown to reduce phosphate in fulgurites and iron silicides have been reported and reviewed in fulgurite contexts. Background: What Fulgurites Are A fulgurite is a natural melt product produced when lightning delivers enough energy into a substrate to fuse, vitrify, and sometimes vaporize mineral grains. In silica-rich settings, the resulting material is commonly dominated by lechatelierite, amorphous silica glass. The morphology and chemistry of a fulgurite depend on the struck substrate, the discharge conditions, moisture, organic content, metal contamination, and cooling history. This matters because fulgurites are not uniform laboratory glasses. They are small, violent, heterogeneous melt products. A single specimen can contain clean silica glass, mixed groundmass, bubbles, charred residues, metallic inclusions, weathered exterior surfaces, and cracks that later admit fluids or contaminants. That heterogeneity is exactly why nitrogen provenance must be resolved before interpretation. The chemistry question is not simply: «Is there nitrogen?» The better question is: «Where is the nitrogen, what chemical form is it in, and how do we know it belongs to the lightning event rather than to later contamination or biological/weathering overprint?» --- 3. The Actual Gap Fulgurites can preserve event information. That is not the speculative part. The sealed-vesicle gas result is already real enough to treat as a target for replication: Navarro-González and colleagues reported CO₂, CO, and NO trapped inside glassy bubbles in a Libyan Desert fulgurite and used those gases, plus isotopic and C/N information, to infer paleoecological context. Lightning-driven redox chemistry is also a real lane. Pasek and Block reported that cloud-to-ground lightning can reduce phosphate in fulgurites, with reduced phosphorus found in several specimens. Iron silicides have also been reviewed in fulgurite occurrences, with the key issue being the extremely reducing microenvironments required for their formation. The gap is more specific: «Positive nitrogen signals in fulgurites are easy to overinterpret unless they are assigned to the correct reservoir.» A nitrogen peak, by itself, is not a structural claim. A surface nitrate signal is not event nitrogen. A CN signal is not automatically lattice nitrogen. A SiN⁻ secondary ion in SIMS is not automatically proof of a pre-existing Si–N bond. A bubble gas signal is not the same as a bonded network signal. The chemistry lane is therefore a sorting machine. --- 4. Why Structural Si–N Is Not Expected Structural Si–N in ordinary fulgurite glass is a predicted negative. That is the central chemistry claim. The argument has four parts. 4.1 Nitrogen speciation in silicate melts is redox-controlled Nitrogen incorporation in silicate melts depends strongly on oxygen fugacity. Under relatively oxidizing conditions, nitrogen is generally present as molecular N₂ rather than as network-bonded nitride. Under highly reducing conditions, nitride-like N³⁻ species can become more significant and enter melt structures. That means ordinary air-formed lightning glass is not the natural setting where one should expect structural nitride or silicon oxynitride formation. 4.2 Ordinary fulgurites form in air Most terrestrial fulgurites form when lightning strikes sand, soil, rock, or sediment in the atmosphere. That setting is not a deliberately reducing furnace, not an ammonia treatment, and not a nitride-starting-material synthesis environment. Even if tiny reduced microzones form locally, the broad prior remains: structural Si–N in clean silica glass should be absent or below meaningful detection. 4.3 Silicon oxynitride requires special conditions Natural silicon oxynitride, known as sinoite, was identified as a meteoritic mineral in an enstatite chondrite, a highly reduced extraterrestrial context, not an ordinary terrestrial lightning-glass product. Confirmed terrestrial nitride minerals are exceptionally rare; siderazot, an iron nitride from a fumarolic setting, was historically reported once and only much later confirmed and structurally characterized. The base-rate argument is important: nature can make nitrides, but ordinary struck soil is not the expected place to make structural silicon nitride or silicon oxynitride glass. 4.4 The honest expected result is an upper bound If EELS does not see nitrogen in fresh interior glass, that does not prove “nothing interesting happened.” It means the structural-bonding claim is unsupported and should be reported as an upper bound. Status: predicted negative. R2 — Occluded Molecular Gas Definition: nitrogen-bearing gas trapped inside sealed vesicles, potentially including NO, NOₓ, N₂ mixtures, CO, and CO₂. Prior expectation: plausible and important.
